subject: bio
title: Mitotic Cell Cycle
subtitle: Cell cycle phases, mitosis, meiosis and cancer.
concept: The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2) followed by mitosis (PMAT) and cytokinesis; it produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
DNA replication occurs during the S phase of interphase, producing two identical double-stranded DNA molecules.
Cancer results from uncontrolled cell division due to mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle.

notes.heading: Phases of the Cell Cycle
items: G1 (Gap 1): cell grows; proteins and organelles are synthesised.
S (Synthesis): DNA replication; each chromosome is duplicated into two sister chromatids.
G2 (Gap 2): cell continues to grow; prepares for division; centrosomes replicate.

notes.heading: Stages of Mitosis (PMAT)
items: Prophase: chromosomes condense; spindle forms from centrioles; nuclear envelope breaks down.
Metaphase: chromosomes align at the equator (metaphase plate); spindle fibres attach to centromeres.
Anaphase: centromeres split; sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles by spindle fibres.
Telophase: nuclear envelopes reform around each set of chromosomes; chromosomes decondense.
Cytokinesis: cytoplasm divides — cleavage furrow in animals; cell plate forms in plants.

notes.heading: Significance of Mitosis
items: Produces two genetically identical diploid cells.
Used in: growth, repair, asexual reproduction.

notes.heading: Cancer and the Cell Cycle
items: Proto-oncogenes promote cell division; mutations → oncogenes (over-stimulate division).
Tumour suppressor genes (e.g. p53) halt division if DNA is damaged; mutations remove this brake.
Malignant tumours: cells invade surrounding tissue and metastasise.
Lifestyle factors: UV radiation, carcinogens (e.g. tobacco smoke), viral infection can cause mutations.

definitions.body: Nuclear division producing two genetically identical diploid daughter cells from a single parent cell.
The region of a chromosome that holds two sister chromatids together and to which spindle fibres attach.
A normal gene that promotes cell growth and division; mutation converts it to an oncogene.
A gene that produces proteins which inhibit cell division or promote apoptosis; loss of function leads to uncontrolled division.

workedExamples.q: Explain what happens to DNA content during the S phase and anaphase of mitosis.

steps.text: DNA replication occurs: each DNA molecule is copied semi-conservatively, doubling the DNA content.
Centromeres split and spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles — chromosome number doubles momentarily, but DNA content per cell stays the same until cytokinesis.
Each daughter cell receives the original number of chromosomes; DNA content returns to the pre-S-phase level.

mistakes: Confusing chromatids (two copies of one chromosome, joined at centromere) with chromosomes.
Stating chromosomes replicate in prophase — replication occurs in S phase (interphase).
Forgetting cytokinesis is separate from mitosis (nuclear division).
tips: Learn PMAT: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase — and one key event per stage.
In cancer questions: name specific genes (oncogene, tumour suppressor) and explain loss of control.
Mitosis vs meiosis: mitosis = 2 identical diploid cells; meiosis = 4 genetically different haploid cells.

flashcards.q: In which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?
What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
flashcards.a: Centromeres split; spindle fibres pull sister chromatids to opposite poles of the cell.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a benign and malignant tumour?
flashcards.a: Benign: localised, does not invade. Malignant: invasive, can metastasise (spread to other tissues via blood/lymph).

flashcards.q: What is the role of a tumour suppressor gene?
flashcards.a: Produces proteins that slow or stop cell division, or trigger apoptosis when DNA is damaged.
Two identical copies of a chromosome joined at the centromere, produced by DNA replication during S phase.

flashcards.q: Name the stage of mitosis where chromosomes align at the equator.

questions.q: At which stage do spindle fibres attach to centromeres?
questions.exp: At metaphase, chromosomes align at the equatorial plate and spindle fibres attach to the centromeres.

questions.q: A cell has 46 chromosomes at the start of mitosis. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have?
questions.exp: Mitosis maintains chromosome number — each daughter cell receives 46 chromosomes.

questions.q: Which gene type promotes excessive cell division when mutated?
questions.exp: Oncogenes are mutated proto-oncogenes that stimulate uncontrolled cell division.

questions.q: What occurs during the S phase of interphase?
questions.exp: S = Synthesis phase; DNA is replicated semi-conservatively, producing two identical chromatids per chromosome.

questions.q: A student observes a dividing cell with chromosomes moving to opposite poles. Which stage is this?
questions.exp: Anaphase: centromeres split and chromatids are pulled to opposite poles by spindle fibres.

recall: Describe the stages of the cell cycle.
List the key events of each stage of mitosis.
Explain why DNA content changes during the cell cycle.
Explain how mutations in oncogenes lead to cancer.
Distinguish between mitosis and meiosis in terms of products.
